questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.question: What is the optimal multi-step synthetic sequence to construct the core target structure of Chapter 13?

options.label: A
options.text: Sequential functional group interconversions (FGI) and strategic C-C bond forming steps tailored to Chapter 13 target chemistry.

options.label: B
options.text: Direct single-step combustion with oxygen.

options.label: C
options.text: Uncontrolled free radical cracking at 800°C.

options.label: D
options.text: Dissolving in concentrated acid without reagent control.

questions.correct_answer: Sequential functional group interconversions (FGI) and strategic C-C bond forming steps tailored to Chapter 13 target chemistry.
questions.explanation: Multi-step synthesis combines regioselective and stereospecific transformations to assemble complex Chapter 13 architectures.

questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.question: In the retrosynthetic analysis of Chapter 13 targets, what strategic disconnection reveals the simplest starting materials?

options.label: A
options.text: Cleaving every single C-C bond in the molecule simultaneously.

options.label: B
options.text: Converting all carbons into carbon dioxide synthons.

options.label: C
options.text: Cleaving the most accessible carbon-carbon or carbon-heteroatom bond to identify commercially available Chapter 13 precursors.

options.label: D
options.text: Assuming zero precursor availability.

questions.correct_answer: Cleaving the most accessible carbon-carbon or carbon-heteroatom bond to identify commercially available Chapter 13 precursors.
questions.explanation: Retrosynthesis systematically disconnects key bonds into stabilized synthetic equivalents.

questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.question: When an organometallic Grignard reaction must be performed on a substrate containing a free alcohol in Chapter 13, what protecting strategy is essential?

options.label: A
options.text: Heat the alcohol with concentrated sulfuric acid to destroy it.

options.label: B
options.text: Convert the alcohol into an explosive peroxide.

options.label: C
options.text: Protect the alcohol as a silyl ether (TMSCl / Et₃N) prior to Grignard addition, and deprotect with TBAF in Chapter 13.

options.label: D
options.text: Ignore the alcohol because Grignards do not react with O-H bonds.

questions.correct_answer: Protect the alcohol as a silyl ether (TMSCl / Et₃N) prior to Grignard addition, and deprotect with TBAF in Chapter 13.
questions.explanation: Silyl ethers mask acidic hydroxyl protons, preventing protonation of basic organometallic reagents.

questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.question: How can an aldehyde or ketone carbonyl be temporarily protected against reducing agents (LiAlH₄) during a Chapter 13 synthesis?

options.label: A
options.text: Convert the carbonyl to an alkane with Wolff-Kishner reduction.

options.label: B
options.text: Oxidize the carbonyl to a carboxylic acid.

options.label: C
options.text: Convert the carbonyl into a cyclic acetal using ethylene glycol and catalytic TsOH, and deprotect with aqueous acid (H₃O⁺) in Chapter 13.

options.label: D
options.text: Treat with sodium borohydride.

questions.correct_answer: Convert the carbonyl into a cyclic acetal using ethylene glycol and catalytic TsOH, and deprotect with aqueous acid (H₃O⁺) in Chapter 13.
questions.explanation: Cyclic acetals are stable to strong bases and hydrides, and are easily hydrolyzed back to carbonyls with aqueous acid.

questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.question: How is an ester selectively preserved while an aldehyde in the same molecule is reduced in Chapter 13?

options.label: A
options.text: Using concentrated nitric acid.

options.label: B
options.text: Using catalytic hydrogenation with platinum at 200°C.

options.label: C
options.text: Using excess LiAlH₄ in refluxing ether.

options.label: D
options.text: By treating with sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) in methanol at 0°C, which rapidly reduces aldehydes but is completely inert toward esters in Chapter 13.

questions.correct_answer: By treating with sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) in methanol at 0°C, which rapidly reduces aldehydes but is completely inert toward esters in Chapter 13.
questions.explanation: NaBH₄ exhibits high chemoselectivity for aldehydes/ketones over carboxylic acid derivatives.

questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.question: What synthetic route ensures the stereospecific formation of a cis-disubstituted product in Chapter 13?

options.label: A
options.text: Using thermal cracking.

options.label: B
options.text: Employing stereospecific syn-addition reactions (such as catalytic hydrogenation over Lindlar/Pt or OsO₄ dihydroxylation) in Chapter 13.

options.label: C
options.text: Using free radical halogenation at 250°C.

options.label: D
options.text: Using acid-catalyzed hydration with carbocation rearrangement.

questions.correct_answer: Employing stereospecific syn-addition reactions (such as catalytic hydrogenation over Lindlar/Pt or OsO₄ dihydroxylation) in Chapter 13.
questions.explanation: Concerted syn-additions deliver substituents to the same face with complete stereocontrol.

questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.topic: Ch13 C-C Bond Extension via Alkynylation
questions.question: What two-step sequence extends a primary alkyl halide by two carbons with a terminal alkyne in Chapter 13?

options.label: A
options.text: 1. Treatment with sulfuric acid.

options.label: B
options.text: 1. Treatment with methane gas → 2. UV light.

options.label: C
options.text: 1. Sodium acetylide (NaC≡CH) in liquid NH₃ (SN2 alkylation) → 2. Aqueous workup in Chapter 13.

options.label: D
options.text: 1. Treatment with sodium hydroxide.

questions.correct_answer: 1. Sodium acetylide (NaC≡CH) in liquid NH₃ (SN2 alkylation) → 2. Aqueous workup in Chapter 13.
questions.explanation: Acetylide anions are powerful nucleophiles that displace primary alkyl halides via SN2.

questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.question: What sequence executes the FGI from a primary alcohol to a primary amine in Chapter 13?

options.label: A
options.text: 1. TsCl / Pyridine (tosylation) → 2. Sodium azide (NaN₃) in DMSO (SN2) → 3. LiAlH₄ or H₂/Pd (reduction to primary amine) in Chapter 13.

options.label: B
options.text: 1. Concentrated sulfuric acid at 200°C.

options.label: C
options.text: 1. KMnO₄ oxidation → 2. NaOH.

options.label: D
options.text: 1. Treatment with ammonia gas at 500°C directly.

questions.correct_answer: 1. TsCl / Pyridine (tosylation) → 2. Sodium azide (NaN₃) in DMSO (SN2) → 3. LiAlH₄ or H₂/Pd (reduction to primary amine) in Chapter 13.
questions.explanation: Tosylation activates the alcohol for azide displacement, followed by reduction to yield the pure primary amine without polyalkylation.

questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.question: What is the principle of an 'orthogonal protecting group strategy' in complex Chapter 13 syntheses?

options.label: A
options.text: Using two or more protecting groups that can be removed independently by completely different chemical mechanisms without affecting each other in Chapter 13.

options.label: B
options.text: Avoiding all purification.

options.label: C
options.text: Using protecting groups that permanently destroy the substrate.

options.label: D
options.text: Using identical protecting groups on every functional group.

questions.correct_answer: Using two or more protecting groups that can be removed independently by completely different chemical mechanisms without affecting each other in Chapter 13.
questions.explanation: Orthogonality (e.g., acid-labile Boc vs base-labile Fmoc vs fluoride-labile silyl ether) allows selective deprotection at designated stages.

questions.chapter_title: Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
questions.question: Why is a convergent synthesis connecting two 4-step fragments superior to an 8-step linear synthesis in Chapter 13?

options.label: A
options.text: Convergent synthesis eliminates all carbon atoms.

options.label: B
options.text: Linear synthesis always produces racemic mixtures.

options.label: C
options.text: Convergent coupling minimizes material loss across long sequences, yielding higher overall recovery and simplified purification in Chapter 13.

options.label: D
options.text: Convergent synthesis requires zero reagents.

questions.correct_answer: Convergent coupling minimizes material loss across long sequences, yielding higher overall recovery and simplified purification in Chapter 13.
questions.explanation: Convergent routes maximize overall yield by reducing the number of consecutive sequential steps.

questions.question: When an organometallic Grignard reaction must be performed on a substrate containing a free alcohol in Chapter 13, what protecting strategy is essential?

options.text: Heat the alcohol with concentrated sulfuric acid to destroy it.

options.label: B
options.text: Ignore the alcohol because Grignards do not react with O-H bonds.

options.text: Protect the alcohol as a silyl ether (TMSCl / Et₃N) prior to Grignard addition, and deprotect with TBAF in Chapter 13.

questions.correct_answer: Protect the alcohol as a silyl ether (TMSCl / Et₃N) prior to Grignard addition, and deprotect with TBAF in Chapter 13.

questions.question: What sequence executes the FGI from a primary alcohol to a primary amine in Chapter 13?

options.text: 1. TsCl / Pyridine (tosylation) → 2. Sodium azide (NaN₃) in DMSO (SN2) → 3. LiAlH₄ or H₂/Pd (reduction to primary amine) in Chapter 13.

options.label: C
options.text: 1. KMnO₄ oxidation → 2. NaOH.

questions.explanation: Tosylation activates the alcohol for azide displacement, followed by reduction to yield the pure primary amine without polyalkylation.
